318: The first recognisable stage of the red cell lineage: 14 to 19 µm, large nucleus with fine chromatin, nucleoli, very basophilic cytoplasm. Its survival depends on erythropoietin (EPO), made by the kidney when oxygen is short: EPO-R receptor, JAK2 kinase, STAT5 factor, anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-xL. In a few divisions and about five days it will yield some fifteen to thirty red cells.
320: 12 to 17 µm. Intensely blue cytoplasm with May-Grünwald-Giemsa: it is packed with ribosomes starting to make globins. The transferrin receptor is very abundant and haem synthesis speeds up (ALAS2 in the mitochondrion). The cell you can explore is at this stage.
322: 10 to 15 µm. Haemoglobin (pink) builds up in a cytoplasm still rich in ribosomes (blue): a grey-lilac hue. Chromatin condenses into clumps. This is the last stage able to divide.
324: 8 to 12 µm. Pink cytoplasm, almost saturated with haemoglobin; small, dense, eccentric nucleus. It no longer divides: its nucleus, with highly compacted chromatin, is about to be expelled with a thin rim of cytoplasm, by a mechanism close to an asymmetric division (actin–myosin ring). The cell then becomes a reticulocyte.
326: A condensed nucleus wrapped in a thin layer of cytoplasm and membrane. Within minutes it exposes phosphatidylserine, an “eat me” signal recognised by the central macrophage (notably the MERTK receptor), which engulfs and digests it.
328: A giant cell (often 50 to 100 µm) with a multilobed, polyploid nucleus, up to 64n: under thrombopoietin, DNA replicates without cell division (endomitosis). It pushes long extensions, proplatelets, through the endothelium, and blood flow fragments them into platelets: several thousand per megakaryocyte.
329: An extension of the megakaryocyte reaching into the sinusoid lumen. Microtubules (β1 tubulin) elongate it and convey granules and organelles to its swellings; blood flow detaches them, and these fragments finish dividing into platelets in the circulation.
331: A 50 to 100 µm cell filled by a single triglyceride droplet that pushes nucleus and cytoplasm to the edge. With age, fatty “yellow” marrow gradually replaces haematopoietic “red” marrow, first in the long bones. The marrow adipocyte secretes adiponectin and leptin and influences haematopoiesis.
333: Precursor of neutrophils: 12 to 18 µm, oval or kidney-shaped nucleus, azurophilic granules (myeloperoxidase, elastase) then specific granules (lactoferrin). Stimulated by G-CSF, the marrow produces on the order of 10¹¹ neutrophils per day.
335: About a dozen µm, nucleus with 3–5 lobes. The first leukocyte recruited to a site of infection: it rolls on the endothelium (selectins), stops (β2 integrins), crosses it, engulfs bacteria and kills them (NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase, granule proteases) or traps them in DNA nets (NETs).
337: A stromal cell apposed to the outer face of the sinusoid, whose long processes weave the framework of the marrow. It secretes CXCL12 and SCF (ligand of the KIT receptor), which retain and maintain haematopoietic stem cells: a key element of their niche. It carries the leptin receptor.
339: A small round cell (≈ 8 µm, CD34⁺) lodged near a vessel, in a “niche” that keeps it mostly quiescent. Rare — on the order of one marrow cell in 10,000 to 100,000 — it self-renews and gives rise to all blood lineages. This is the cell that is transplanted.
341: Between the hepatocyte and the sinusoidal capillary, less than a micrometre wide in reality. The endothelium, pierced by fenestrae and lacking a continuous basal lamina, lets plasma bathe the hepatocyte microvilli directly. The yellow spheres are LDL (≈ 22 nm, one apolipoprotein B-100, ≈ 1,500 cholesteryl esters). Stellate cells live here. Licence: spaces are widened so that you can move between the hepatocyte plate and the sinusoids.
343: Wall of the sinusoidal capillary (≈ 10 µm in diameter): an extremely thin endothelium pierced by 100 to 150 nm fenestrae grouped in “sieve plates” (dark dots), with no diaphragm and no continuous basal lamina. Plasma and small lipoproteins (LDL, chylomicron remnants) pass; blood cells and large chylomicrons stay in the lumen. It also clears the blood by endocytosis (scavenger receptors) and secretes BMP6, which controls hepcidin. The ship slips through a fenestra when it is small.
345: Mixed blood: ≈ 75 % comes from the portal vein (oxygen-poor, loaded with nutrients absorbed by the gut) and ≈ 25 % from the hepatic artery. It flows slowly from the portal tract to the central vein; bile flows the opposite way in the canaliculi. The liver receives ≈ 1.5 L of blood per minute, a quarter of cardiac output. The “Travel by blood” button takes you to another organ.
347: The resident macrophage of the liver, anchored in the sinusoid lumen: the largest population of tissue macrophages in the body. It filters blood coming from the gut — bacteria, endotoxins, debris, old red cells — and recycles their iron. Of embryonic origin, it self-maintains in place. When activated it secretes TNF and IL-6: in the hepatocyte, IL-6 triggers the acute-phase response… and HAMP transcription.
349: Lodged in the space of Disse, it wraps the sinusoid with its processes. Its lipid droplets (yellow) store most of the body's vitamin A, as retinyl esters. Under chronic injury (alcohol, viruses, steatosis) it is activated by TGF-β and PDGF, loses its droplets, becomes a myofibroblast and lays down collagen: the engine of fibrosis, then cirrhosis.
351: Hepatocytes (20 to 30 µm) line up in plates one cell thick, bordered by sinusoids on two faces. Between neighbouring cells: tight junctions, gap junctions and the bile canaliculus (green cords). About one in five is binucleate in adults, and many are polyploid. They renew slowly, but can regenerate the liver after a major loss.
353: A granular lymphocyte residing in the sinusoid, in contact with the endothelium and Kupffer cells. Without prior immunisation it destroys infected or tumour cells (perforin, granzymes) and secretes interferon γ. The liver is particularly rich in NK cells.
355: Between the cell bodies lies the neuropil: a felt of axons, dendrites and glial processes, with on the order of a billion synapses per mm³. The ◎ target is a synaptic bouton of our neuron; opposite, across a 20 nm cleft, the dendritic spine of another neuron. The small pairs of beads are BDNF dimers. Licence: the real tissue is compact — membranes are only ≈ 20 nm apart and extracellular space takes up only ≈ 20 % of the volume; it has been greatly thinned out so that you can move through it.
357: An axon or dendrite of another neuron. The cortex is woven from them: each mm³ contains several kilometres of axons and several hundred metres of dendrites. Only a few fibres are drawn.
